items.question: The shift from the Planning Commission to NITI Aayog reflects a change in India's development philosophy. Critically examine.
items.modelAnswer:
The replacement of the **Planning Commission (1950)** by **NITI Aayog (2015)** marks a transition from **centralised, directive planning** to **collaborative, indicative policymaking**, mirroring the deeper shift from a command economy to a liberalised, market-driven one after 1991.

The Planning Commission, a **non-statutory body chaired by the PM**, framed successive **Five-Year Plans**, set national priorities and — crucially — **allocated central funds** to states. In a mixed economy with a dominant public sector this served India well: the First Plan built irrigation (Bhakra-Nangal), the Second laid a heavy-industry base (Mahalanobis), and later plans drove the Green Revolution and poverty programmes. But its **top-down, one-size-fits-all** model drew growing criticism — rigidity in a fast-changing global economy, bureaucratic delays, inadequate state consultation (straining centre-state relations), and limited space for the private sector that had become the engine of post-1991 growth.

**NITI Aayog** answers these gaps as a **think-tank and policy advisor** rather than a fund-allocator (devolution now rests with the **Finance Commission**). Its **Governing Council of Chief Ministers** institutionalises **cooperative and competitive federalism**, treating states as equal partners; its **3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy and 15-Year Vision** replace rigid plans; and initiatives like the **Aspirational Districts Programme, SDG India Index and Atal Innovation Mission** embed data-driven, outcome-based governance.

Critically, NITI Aayog's **loss of fund-allocation power** limits its leverage over states, and it has been faulted as more advisory than transformative. Yet its flexibility suits a diversified economy, and it now anchors the **Viksit Bharat @2047** vision. On balance, the shift is a philosophical move from **control to collaboration**, from **allocation to facilitation** — appropriate for a liberalised India, provided cooperative federalism is matched by real fiscal empowerment of states such as Andhra Pradesh.
keyPoints: Planning Commission (1950): non-statutory, PM-chaired, framed Five-Year Plans and allocated funds; top-down and centralised.
Criticisms: rigidity post-1991, bureaucratic delays, weak state consultation, limited private-sector role.
NITI Aayog (2015): think-tank/advisor, no fund allocation (now with Finance Commission), cooperative & competitive federalism.
NITI tools: 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy, 15-Year Vision; Aspirational Districts, SDG India Index, Atal Innovation Mission.
Balanced view: greater flexibility and state partnership, but weaker leverage; anchors Viksit Bharat @2047.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Economics: Planning in India (Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog)

items.question: Assess the objectives and achievements of India's Five-Year Plans. To what extent did the underlying growth models shape their outcomes?
items.modelAnswer:
India's **Five-Year Plans (1951-2017)** pursued four enduring objectives — **growth, equity, modernisation and self-reliance** — through a **centralised, public-sector-led** strategy inspired by socialist planning.

The **growth models** decisively shaped outcomes. The **First Plan** applied the **Harrod-Domar model**, tying growth to saving and investment; with heavy investment in agriculture and irrigation it **exceeded its target (3.6% vs 2.1%)** and delivered Bhakra-Nangal and IIT Kharagpur. The **Second Plan** adopted the **Mahalanobis model**, betting on **heavy capital-goods industries** — Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur steel plants — and building a mixed economy, though at the cost of forex shortages and neglect of consumer goods and employment. The **Third Plan's Gadgil-Yojana** aimed at self-reliance but **collapsed** under the 1962 and 1965 wars and drought, forcing the **Plan Holiday (1966-69)** and the Green Revolution pivot of the Fourth Plan.

Achievements are substantial: **food self-sufficiency** via the Green Revolution, an **industrial and PSU base**, institutional capacity, and, after the **Eighth Plan's LPG turn (1992-97)**, higher growth (6.8%). Later plans (Eleventh onward) reframed the goal as **'faster and more inclusive growth'** with health, education and MGNREGA.

Yet the model choices also entrenched weaknesses — an **industry-first bias** that underplayed jobs and agriculture, persistent **regional disparities and poverty**, and inefficiency in protected PSUs. The **Twelfth Plan (2012-17)** was the last, as rigid multi-year targeting gave way to NITI Aayog's flexible vision documents. In sum, growth models were not neutral: **Harrod-Domar** made the First Plan investment-led, **Mahalanobis** made the economy industry-heavy, and their assumptions explain both the plans' signal successes and their structural shortfalls — a lesson relevant to state planning in Andhra Pradesh today.
keyPoints: Objectives: growth, equity, modernisation, self-reliance under centralised public-sector-led planning.
Harrod-Domar (First Plan) → investment-led, agriculture; exceeded target at 3.6%.
Mahalanobis (Second Plan) → heavy industry & steel plants; forex shortages, weak on jobs.
Gadgil-Yojana (Third Plan) failed (wars/drought) → Plan Holiday → Green Revolution (Fourth Plan).
Achievements: food self-sufficiency, industrial/PSU base; Eighth Plan LPG raised growth to 6.8%.
Weaknesses: industry bias, regional disparities, persistent poverty; Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last.
